blocks.title: A finite check cannot settle an infinite size claim
paragraphs: For finite sets, counting elements compares size. For infinite sets, a listing or bijection must account for every element, with a reason that no element is missed. This lesson stays within the normalized number-set, countability, Cantor and paradox overview.

blocks.title: Number-set membership and hierarchy
paragraphs: The hierarchy is ℕ⊆ℤ⊆ℚ⊆ℝ⊆ℂ: natural numbers, integers, rationals, reals and complex numbers. Here natural-number indexing is stated explicitly as ℕ₀={0,1,2,…}; another task may start natural numbers at 1. A rational has the form p/q with integers p,q and q≠0.

For example, −3 belongs to ℤ,ℚ,ℝ,ℂ but not ℕ₀; 3/2 belongs to ℚ,ℝ,ℂ but not ℤ; i belongs to ℂ but not ℝ. Membership in several nested number sets is consistent, so “which sets?” may have several answers.

A set’s elements and its cardinality are different questions. ℕ₀ and ℤ are distinct sets, yet have the same infinite cardinality. ℚ is also countably infinite, while ℝ is uncountable; adjoining an imaginary component gives ℂ, which is uncountable as well.

blocks.title: Give a rule and prove it covers the set
paragraphs: A set is countably infinite if there is a bijection with ℕ₀. A finite set is also called countable under the at-most-countable convention used here; keep this distinction explicit.

A listing of ℤ is 0,1,−1,2,−2,3,−3,… . Define f(0)=0, f(2k−1)=k, and f(2k)=−k for integers k≥1. Positive integers occupy odd positive indices; negative integers occupy even positive indices. Zero occupies index zero.

Every integer has exactly one described index, which proves both coverage and no duplicates. The visible beginning of the list is only an illustration; the rule and its justification establish the infinite claim.

blocks.title: Avoid missing elements and uncontrolled duplicates
paragraphs: To list positive rationals, arrange pairs (p,q) of positive integers by increasing p+q and within each diagonal by increasing p. Output p/q only when it has not appeared earlier, equivalently when the pair is in lowest terms. Every positive rational has such a pair at a finite diagonal.

Insert zero and interleave positive entries with their negatives to cover ℚ. A countability explanation must justify that every target is reached after finitely many steps and handle duplicate representations such as 1/2 and 2/4. A few enumerated fractions are not that proof.

blocks.title: A diagonal defeats a proposed complete list
paragraphs: For any proposed function f:A→𝒫(A), form D={a∈A | a∉f(a)}. If f were surjective, some d∈A would satisfy f(d)=D. Then d∈D exactly when d∉D, a contradiction. Thus no such function lists every subset of A.

The point is not that one particular list failed: the construction works against any proposed surjection. For A=ℕ₀, it shows 𝒫(ℕ₀) cannot be counted by a natural-number listing. This course-depth diagonal argument does not require advanced cardinal arithmetic.

blocks.title: State the boundary a paradox exposes
paragraphs: Unrestricted set formation is unsafe. If a universal collection R={x | x∉x} were itself a set to which the condition applied, asking whether R∈R gives R∈R exactly when R∉R. That contradiction shows why one cannot treat every unrestricted condition as defining a set.

Keep the scope of the conclusion precise: the paradox challenges unrestricted set formation; it does not show that ordinary set calculations are all invalid. Likewise, failure of a proposed proof or finite search is not automatically a theorem about impossibility.

The normalized source identifies a limitations overview but does not supply exact theorem formulations for a broader formal-systems course. No completeness, decidability or independence theorem beyond this stated overview is asserted here.

blocks.title: Distinguish an argument from an illustration
paragraphs: Printing many elements cannot verify an infinite bijection. Give a rule and prove that each permitted object has the required unique position. Do not equate “infinite” with “uncountable” or infer a future exam’s scope from a historical occurrence.
Countability proofs and explanations of limitations need a logical review. The practice calculation on fixed number membership is a bounded item, not an automatic check of an infinite proof.

blocks.title: Account for every element and state what follows
paragraphs: Use number-set definitions precisely. For countability, establish a complete listing or bijection rather than a finite sample. For diagonal and paradox arguments, explain the contradiction and the exact assumption it refutes.

cards.prompt: Can one number belong to several of ℕ,ℤ,ℚ,ℝ,ℂ?
cards.answer: Yes. The sets are nested. Declare whether natural numbers start at 0 or 1, then use the definitions and inclusion hierarchy.

cards.prompt: What must a listing argument establish beyond its first few terms?
cards.answer: A rule that reaches every target after finitely many steps, with duplicate handling. For a claimed bijection, also show each target has exactly one index.

cards.prompt: How do “countable” and “countably infinite” differ here?
cards.answer: Countable means finite or admitting a bijection with ℕ₀. Countably infinite excludes finite sets and requires such a bijection.

cards.prompt: Why does D={a∈A | a∉f(a)} obstruct a surjection f:A→𝒫(A)?
cards.answer: If D=f(d), then d∈D iff d∉D, a contradiction. Since f was arbitrary, no function of that type can be surjective.

cards.prompt: What does the self-membership paradox warn against?
cards.answer: Assuming every unrestricted condition defines a set. The contradictory assumption concerns unrestricted set formation, not the validity of every ordinary set argument.

guided.title: Justify an infinite listing
guided.prompt: Show that the listing 0,1,−1,2,−2,… gives a bijection from ℕ₀ to ℤ. Give the rule, not only more terms.
rubric: The definition covers index zero, odd positive indices and even positive indices.
Zero, positive integers and negative integers each have an explicit preimage.
The cases are disjoint and the formulas give unique indices.
reference: Use f(0)=0, f(2k−1)=k and f(2k)=−k for k≥1. The preimage of k>0 is 2k−1, and of −k<0 is 2k.
Each integer has exactly one preimage, so the function is a bijection. A finite output list alone would not prove this.

guided.title: Explain the diagonal contradiction
guided.prompt: Suppose f:A→𝒫(A) is claimed to be surjective. Explain why D={a∈A | a∉f(a)} cannot equal f(d) for any d∈A, and state the precise conclusion.

fields.label: The subset D and the surjectivity assumption

rubric: D is a subset of A and therefore an allowed target of the claimed surjection.
If D=f(d), the defining membership condition becomes d∈D iff d∉D.
The argument applies to any proposed f; it is not a test of a few finite entries.
reference: Surjectivity would supply d with f(d)=D. Substitution in the definition yields the contradiction d∈D iff d∉D.
Consequently no function from A to its powerset is surjective. The explanation is an unscored proof self-check.
